title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content, specifically a fabricated article depicting a fake interview, was used to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The failure did not occur inside a legitimate AI deployment; it occurred in the deliberate misuse of AI tools to produce convincing fake text and, by extension, deepfake material featuring real public figures. The fabricated content was designed to exploit the credibility of recognized individuals, including a central bank governor and a finance presenter, to make an investment scam appear credible.

The scale reported by ASIC points to a systematic pattern rather than isolated incidents. The regulator removed tens of thousands of schemes in a single year, a figure that suggests automated or semi-automated production of fraudulent content at a volume that outpaces manual detection. Catching this class of fraud requires verification at the distribution layer, meaning the platforms and advertising networks that carry the fake articles and endorsements, because the content itself is constructed to pass casual inspection.

What is not established is any finding of criminal liability against specific individuals or organizations behind the platform named in the fake article, and the reporting from regulators and news outlets does not constitute proof of who created the content or how it was technically produced.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake article circulating online falsely depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never actually occurred. This fabricated content represents a growing category of scam that uses artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and fake news articles featuring well-known Australians. The corporate regulator ASIC reports these AI-generated investment schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and harder to detect.

ASIC's latest research reveals a significant rise in investment scams, with the regulator removing 19,400 schemes last year, a 182 percent increase. The agency took down 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and finance presenter Alan Kohler rank among the most commonly impersonated Australians, alongside politicians like Pauline Hanson and business figures including Dick Smith and Gina Rinehart. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial service licenses and avoid investing based on celebrity endorsements or online testimonials, as scammers build elaborate webs of fake websites, reviews, and advertisements to deceive potential investors.
